thread.title: Tesla Rose on Musk’s Apology, but Bad Boy CEOs Are Here to Stay

author: Teresa Rivas
title: Tesla Rose on Musk’s Apology, but Bad Boy CEOs Are Here to Stay
text:
By Teresa Rivas Aug. 3, 2018 11:14 a.m. ET Shares of Tesla (TSLA) have been on a tear since the company's second-quarter earnings report, helped along by the company update and an apology from its CEO for his conduct during last quarter's conference call.
Where we were: Tesla shares had been on a downward slide before the report, given no shortage of negative headlines about the company. Where we're headed: Rude CEOs may never disappear, but it's up to investors to decide how much weight to put on their behavior. Illustration: Mark Brake/Getty Images All's well that ends well. That's what Shakespeare titled one of his tragicomic plays, and the same could be said of Tesla (TSLA), as despite a spate of bad news, the stock soared after its second-quarter earnings and CEO Elon Musk' s mea culpa and promise of better behavior .
Yet the Bard was no stranger to salty language and insults ("I bite my thumb at you!"), so its unlikely he would have blinked an eye at Tesla's now infamous first-quarter earnings call , when Musk insulted analysts and cut off questions. Neither did Datatrek 's Nicolas Colas : He writes that he's been verbally berated and abused by plenty of auto executives in the course of duty as an equity analyst (not to mention getting death threats from clients).
His conclusion? "Elon's not really all that rude." At least on a comparative basis. Colas writes that Musk's comments weren't really all that outlandish, but that it's not surprising that the stock was still rewarded for his apology. After all, at this point, "the actions of senior managements are the only remaining unknown that can profoundly affect stock prices," given that so much other fundamental analysis has been automated.
While analysts ( like rappers ) might come away with hurt feelings, and the stock may occasionally suffer, Colas believes that the "age of the Prickly CEO," which began with Apple 's (AAPL) Steve Jobs , is far from over. Founders may be more prone to this behavior, given their bigger stakes in the outcome, and tech has plenty of founder-controlled companies, which compounds the issue. (Then of course there's the fact that psychopathy is more common among CEOs .)
Colas concludes that it will be impossible to separate the good from the bad. "People have betas, just like stocks. Rudeness merely signals that underlying volatility is different from the average manager. It is up to analysts, portfolio managers, and markets to determine if it comes with a valuable vision or just masks weakness." Sometimes it does, and sometimes it doesn't.
Indeed, this may not be the end of the stock doing well: Tesla is higher today, gaining 1.1% to $353.41. But perhaps Musk learned another lesson: The ends don't always justify the means. Maybe, especially in today's world, it pays to be nice.
